lesson.title: Like Terms: Knowing What You're Allowed to Combine
lesson.summary: Like terms are terms that share the exact same variable or variables raised to the exact same exponents, and only like terms can be combined by adding or subtracting their coefficients.
lesson.body:
A term is a single piece of an expression, a number, a variable, or a product of numbers and variables, that sits between the plus and minus signs of the expression. In the expression 5x^2 + 3x - 7x^2 + 2 - x + 9, the terms are 5x^2, 3x, -7x^2, 2, -x, and 9, each one carrying its own sign along with it. Like terms are any two terms that have exactly the same variable part, meaning the same variables raised to the exact same exponents. The numerical coefficient in front is allowed to differ between like terms, but the variable part, including every exponent, has to match precisely.

The reason like terms can be combined comes straight from the distributive property in reverse. Adding 5x^2 and -7x^2 works the same way as adding 5 apples and negative 7 apples, since x^2 is playing the role of a common unit being counted: 5x^2 + (-7x^2) = (5 + (-7))x^2 = -2x^2. This only makes sense because both terms are counting the exact same unit, x^2. You cannot combine 5x^2 with 3x in this way, because x^2 and x are different units entirely, one representing x multiplied by itself and the other representing a single factor of x, a distinction that comes directly from how exponents were defined earlier in this unit.

Apply this to the full expression 5x^2 + 3x - 7x^2 + 2 - x + 9. First, sort the terms into groups of like terms: the x^2 terms are 5x^2 and -7x^2, the x terms are 3x and -x, and the constant terms are 2 and 9. Combine each group separately. The x^2 terms give 5x^2 - 7x^2 = -2x^2. The x terms give 3x - x = 2x, since -x is understood to have a coefficient of -1, so 3x + (-1x) = 2x. The constants give 2 + 9 = 11. Putting the simplified groups back together gives -2x^2 + 2x + 11.

You can verify this simplification is correct by substituting a specific value for x into both the original expression and the simplified one, then checking that they match, using the substitution and evaluating skills from the last two lessons. Try x = 2. In the original expression: 5(2)^2 + 3(2) - 7(2)^2 + 2 - 2 + 9 = 5(4) + 6 - 7(4) + 2 - 2 + 9 = 20 + 6 - 28 + 2 - 2 + 9 = 7. In the simplified expression: -2(2)^2 + 2(2) + 11 = -2(4) + 4 + 11 = -8 + 4 + 11 = 7. Both give 7, confirming the two expressions are equivalent.

A final caution: the order of variables multiplied together does not affect whether terms are like terms, since multiplication can be done in any order, so xy and yx are like terms and can be combined. But watch the exponents closely, because xy and xy^2 are not like terms, even though both involve only x and y, since the exponent on y differs between them, 1 in the first case and 2 in the second.

Combining like terms never changes the value an expression produces for a given input, it only changes how compactly that value is written, which is exactly why the substitution check above works as proof. This is also why like terms sit at the foundation of nearly every simplification you will do from here forward: whenever an expression has more terms than it needs, sorting them by matching variable parts and collapsing each group into one term is almost always the first productive move to make.
